latest_post.title: Government says No: big cuts in Durham and Westminster
latest_post.author: Ian Anstice / The Library Campaign

editorial.text: The Government has announced that it will not be giving any extra funding to libraries. It comprehensively rejected Education Select Committee recommendations that required any money and only was willing to consider any recommendations that would come free of charge. So, since 2010 it seems, no matter what government, whatever new prime minister we get, it seems that there’s no meaningful change to the approach to the public library sector. The overall message was very much, in the words of the Emperor Honorius when he officially recognised the loss of Britannia to the Roman Empire, “Look to your own defence”. Well, we all know how that went. Leading the way this week to the new Dark Ages are Durham and Westminster who both announced major cuts to library services, with a £1.2m and £600k cut respectively. This appears to represent a cut of around a quarter to each service. Elsewhere, the Vandals are already firmly established in at least two other outposts. The British Library has partially set aside its whole point of being due to financial pressures and has decided that two of its public reading rooms – paid for entirely by public money – are actually private commercial meeting room lets. It is also replacing managing its own security guards (legionaries in this extended metaphor) with private company security (barbarian mercenaries?). And then we get to the new heathen kingdom of Staffordshire (think the East Coast in around 500 AD) where the Reform Council have formally agreed that only they get to decide what politically neutral library events and displays are. They have courteously allowed that Holocaust Memorial Day is OK. Of course, this presumably only means politically neutral holocausts. I imagine there’ll be no coverage in the county of what has happened in Palestine any time soon. Everything is political, Councillor Attila, and you know that. Finally, the question of what to do with David Walliams books seems to be settling down, with publicly available declarations showing 42 councils not removing his books, 3 removing and – bless – one not being able to make up its mind yet. Pembrokeshire, you’ve got this, be strong. Just don’t invite in any Angle, Saxon or Jute consultants in for your new collections management policy. Authorities not removing Walliams – Bolton, Bracknell Forest, Bristol, Calderdale, Cambridgeshire, Cornwall, Durham, East Lothian, East Sussex, Essex, Falkirk, Flintshire, Gateshead, Gloucestershire, Guernsey, Hampshire, Hartlepool, Hertfordshire, Inverclyde, Isle of Wight, Jersey, Kent, Liverpool, Medway, Newcastle, Norfolk, North Tyneside, Northern Ireland, Northumberland, Portsmouth, Somerset, South Tyneside, Suffolk, Surrey, Swindon, Torfaen, Waltham Forest, Westmorland & Furness, West Sussex, Wiltshire, Wokingham, Wrexham, York. Total = 42 Authorities removing: Camden, Monmouthshire, Telford & Wrekin. Total = 3 Not made up their minds – Pembrokeshire

stories.text: British Library. New Chief Executive explains the reasoning behind the unpopular introduction of charging for reading rooms. “The Library is running a financial deficit. Our real-terms government funding has reduced by a third compared to 2010. This year we expect to spend around £7 million more than our total income. Without taking action, our recurring deficit is forecast to grow to over £8 million next year (2027–28) and nearly £11 million the year after.” … “We estimate that the new workspace will generate around £3.5m annually by year three of operation, rising to over £4.5m by year 10, to invest back into Library services. The reallocation of the three Reading Rooms won’t solve all our financial challenges, but it is a substantial part of the solution and eases the need for much more painful savings.” see also Corporate Greed Will Kill the British Library – Tribune. “The British Library’s attempt to turn reading rooms into business spaces and outsource workers is an act of gross cultural vandalism — which will be resisted by a workforce who understand their worth.” … “In the face of this drive towards the maximisation of profit at the expense of public knowledge, the British Library staff aren’t flinching. They are united around a much deeper, radical understanding of their work’s purpose, and understand that the wider public appreciate and support their stance. They will continue to acquire, catalogue, curate, conserve, protect, retrieve and deliver collection items to make them publicly accessible and free of charge for all. This is what their fight is about.” and British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces – Guardian. Almost seventy “Guards told their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor that has rejected union recognition” .. PCS unions says “What on earth is a government department doing investing in a resource only to privatise it, and outsourcing workers and stripping them of union recognition?””

stories.text: Government Response – UK Parliament. Government rejects Education Select Committee recommendations where they would increase in cost, partially accepting some others that have no cost implication. Recommendation for restoring funding to public libraries lost since 2010 and rejects another recommendation for the return of library standards, as this would cost too much. Government partially accepts recommendations that have no cost implication, such as improving data links between schools and public libraries, and encouraging school visits. Repeatedly mentions the £150k given by government to the National Year of Reading and suggests “collective action” instead of anything from Government. see also “A missed opportunity to turn warm words into action” – Libraries Connected. ” we are disappointed that recognition has not been matched by investment. The Government has rejected the Committee’s call to restore funding for public libraries and provide outreach officers in every library service. And of the £32.65 million of funding announced during the National Year of Reading, less than 0.5% is for public libraries. Libraries can sometimes be taken for granted, but they are the critical social infrastructure that makes free access to reading possible in every community – last year, in England alone, they lent almost 100 million books.” and Government rejects committee’s call to restore lost library funding – Arts Professional and Disappointment as government stops short of backing National Decade of Reading – BookSeller.
